title: Truth, justice, peace (Avot 1:18)
hookLine: the world endures on three things: truth, justice and peace
carry: justice that makes peace in the gates

cards: A three-legged stool sits steady even on an uneven floor, as long as all three legs are there. Take one away and it doesn't wobble. It falls.
Chapter one of Pirkei Avot started, back with Simon the Just, by naming three things the world stands on: Torah, worship and kindness.
Now, at the very end of the chapter, after the whole chain of teachers, another sage names three more. A second stool.

teach.b: The sage is Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, and his saying closes chapter one. The world endures on three things: on justice, on truth, and on peace.
Then he gives a verse from the prophet Zechariah, who tells the people to judge with truth, and with a justice that makes peace, in their gates. All three in one line of scripture.

Notice the difference from the start of the chapter. Simon the Just said what the world stands on, the reasons it exists at all. This saying is about what keeps it going day to day, in courts and markets and kitchens.

teach.h: THE THREE HOLD EACH OTHER UP.
teach.b: One way to read it: the three hold each other up. Justice without truth is just power. Truth without peace can be a weapon.

Peace without justice is only quiet. A teaching in the Jerusalem Talmud goes further: the three are really one thing, because when real justice is done, truth is done and peace is made. Now today's word.

teach.h: EMET: FROM FIRST LETTER TO LAST.
teach.b: Truth, in Hebrew, is emet, spelled with three letters: alef, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, mem, near the middle, and tav, the very last. The rabbis noticed, and read it as truth that runs from beginning to end.
And the Talmud calls truth God's own seal.

teach.h: TRUTH AND PEACE IN YOUR GATES.
teach.b: That's a lot of weight on one small word. It's also a very ordinary one, the word Hebrew speakers use to say, really? Emet?

how: Jewish teaching treats truthfulness, fair judgment and peacemaking as linked duties, and the three are learned together from this saying, which closes the first chapter of Pirkei Avot.

o: only saying things you could prove in court
being blunt, whoever happens to get hurt by it
emet: honesty that holds from beginning to end

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: from the first letter to the last

s: chapter one of Avot ends with three things the world endures on
justice, truth and peace, from Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel.
this is the same list as Simon the Just's three pillars
Simon named Torah, worship and kindness. this is a second set of three.
the word emet begins with the first Hebrew letter and ends with the last
alef and tav, with mem near the middle, and the rabbis took notice.

games.q: a friend asks what you really think of a plan you know will fail. what do you do?
o: say it's great. keep the peace.
tell them the truth, fairly and gently.
tell them bluntly. truth is truth.
games.why: Rabban Simeon names truth, justice and peace together. a teaching in the Jerusalem Talmud says the three are really one.

practice: Think of something true you've been avoiding saying, to a friend, a partner, a boss, a parent: not a weapon or a lecture, just a true thing. Ask how it could come out with peace in it too, fair to them and gentle.
Let the words get simpler and softer with each breath, without letting them stop being true.
